<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs
</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jihun Kim
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>POSTECH, pohang, Republic of Korea
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Namhoon Lee
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>POSTECH, pohang, Republic of Korea
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:namhoon.lee@postech.ac.kr">namhoon.lee@postech.ac.kr</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">This work presents a new approach to decentralized training—<span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood—designed to scale for large models across complex network topologies and achieve global consensus with minimal communication overhead.
Traditional gossip-based methods suffer from message communication costs that grow with model size, while information decay over network hops renders global consensus inefficient.
<span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood departs from these practices by exploiting the seed-reconstructible structure of zeroth-order updates and effectively making the messages near-zero in size, allowing them to be flooded to every client in the network.
This mechanism makes communication overhead negligible and independent of model size, removing the primary scalability bottleneck in decentralized training.
Consequently, <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood enables training in regimes previously considered impractical, such as billion-parameter models distributed across hundreds of clients.
Our experiments on decentralized LLM fine-tuning demonstrate that <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="abstract1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood consistently outperforms gossip-based baselines in both generalization performance and communication efficiency, and even achieves results comparable to first-order methods in large-scale settings.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18181v1/teaser.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/282;" width="476" height="282"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Task performance vs. Total communication cost plot of different decentralized training methods.
<span id="S1.F1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.F1.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood (<math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bigstar" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#B80000;" mathcolor="#B80000" mathvariant="normal">★</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bigstar</annotation></semantics></math>) is extremely efficient—with <math id="S1.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S1.F1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10^{7}\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>7</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{7}\times</annotation></semantics></math> less communication bytes–while maintaining a reasonable performance level compared to its rivals and strong-but-impractical baseline methods.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Decentralized training enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a shared model while communicating only with neighboring nodes in a network graph, without relying on a central server <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lian et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
This paradigm offers key advantages over centralized federated learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">McMahan et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, including improved robustness to single-point failures, better scalability of communication traffic, and stronger data locality guarantees <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gabrielli et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite its advantages, decentralized training scales poorly with model size due to the substantial communication overhead of standard consensus mechanisms.
This limitation stems from the requirement that local models remain synchronized to avoid divergence; current practices enforce this through gossip-based averaging, which necessitates the frequent exchange of high-dimensional weights or gradients across the network <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lian et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We identify this scalability crisis as two-fold.
First, the communication overhead of gossip-based protocols grows linearly with model dimensionality; for billion-parameter models, a single synchronization step becomes prohibitively expensive under realistic bandwidth constraints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Second, gossip relies on the multi-hop propagation of information, which is inherently slow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vogels et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
As network topologies become larger or sparser, information effectively decays across hops.
This prevents distant nodes from reaching timely consensus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aketi et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, leading to persistent consensus error and degraded model performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kong et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These dual challenges—scalability with respect to both model size and network topology—present a fundamental trade-off that is difficult to resolve within the gossip framework.
For example, efforts to reduce per-round communication via compression often weaken consensus, leading to slower convergence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aketi et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Conversely, strengthening consensus through multiple gossip iterations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hashemi et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2023</a>)</cite> or gradient tracking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koloskova et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2022</a>)</cite> significantly inflates the total communication cost.
Consequently, gossip-based methods remain largely impractical for decentralized training of large-scale models in real-world network environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Meanwhile, recent advances in zeroth-order optimization reveals a significant, yet overlooked, opportunity for decentralized training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Unlike first-order methods, zeroth-order updates can be disseminated without transmitting high-dimensional gradient vectors.
By leveraging shared randomness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, the perturbation directions used in zeroth-order estimates can be reconstructed deterministically from a small random seed.
Consequently, the communication payload is reduced to a constant-size scalar and its associated seed, allowing for the transmission of exact updates without the approximation or compression errors inherent in traditional gradient-reduction techniques.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">This property fundamentally alters the communication landscape.
When updates are seed-reconstructible, model dimensionality ceases to be the primary bottleneck.
Yet, current zeroth-order-based decentralized frameworks still adhere to the gossip paradigm, inheriting its structural consensus limitations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hajinezhad et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
This reveals a critical gap in the literature and prompts a fundamental question:</p>
<p id="S1.p6.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><em id="S1.p6.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">If the communication cost is rendered negligible, why continue to rely on the slow dissemination of gossip at all?</em></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In response, we propose <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood, a decentralized training framework that replaces gossip-based averaging with global dissemination.
Rather than performing local averaging, <span id="S1.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.p7.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood broadcasts each zeroth-order update globally across the entire network based on a recursive flooding mechanism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kshemkalyani and Singhal, 2011</a>)</cite>: upon the first receipt of an update, a client forwards it to all immediate neighbors, who in turn propagate it to their own neighbors.
This chain of transmission continues until the propagation has spanned the network diameter, ensuring that every update generated in a given iteration reaches every client.
This process effectively realizes an all-gather-equivalent consensus at every step without transmitting high-dimensional tensors, even in arbitrary sparse topologies.
Consequently, <span id="S1.p7.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.p7.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood resolves both scalability bottlenecks: communication overhead becomes independent of model size, and consensus quality remains invariant to network distance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">However, communicating via seed-reconstructible updates introduces a new challenge: each client must process a large volume of zeroth-order updates per iteration.
Naively reconstructing and applying these updates individually would incur prohibitive computational overhead <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
To mitigate this, we restrict perturbations to a shared low-rank subspace that is globally synchronized across all clients.
By mapping each zeroth-order update to a specific canonical coordinate within this shared subspace, we can aggregate the entire batch of updates using efficient, vectorized matrix operations rather than iterative reconstruction.
This ensures that the computational cost of reaching consensus remains manageable, even as the number of clients grows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">We summarize our contributions as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:2ex;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood framework</span>: We propose <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood, a decentralized training paradigm that replaces traditional gossip with a flooding-based dissemination mechanism. By exploiting seed-reconstructible updates, <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood achieves near-zero communication overhead and topology-invariant, all-gather-equivalent consensus, effectively removing model dimensionality as a scalability bottleneck.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">Efficient gradient estimator</span>: We introduce a computationally efficient zeroth-order gradient estimator designed for high-throughput update aggregation. By restricting perturbations to a synchronized low-rank subspace, this approach enables clients to aggregate global updates via vectorized matrix operations, mitigating the computational burden of processing high volumes of disseminated seeds.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">Empirical validation</span>: We subject <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood to extensive evaluation, benchmarking decentralized LLM fine-tuning—scaling to 1B parameters across 128 clients.
Our results demonstrate that <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood consistently outperforms gossip-based methods and, in large or sparse network regimes, even surpasses the performance of first-order baselines in decentralized training.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Decentralized Training</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, we consider a set of <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> clients indexed by <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in\{1,\dots,n\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in\{1,\dots,n\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Each client <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> holds a private local dataset <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> which can not be shared.
The goal of decentralized training is to minimize the global objective, defined as the average of all local objectives:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\;F(\theta):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}}\big[f(\theta;\mathcal{B})\big]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.447em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\;F(\theta):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}}\big[f(\theta;\mathcal{B})\big]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the average model parameters and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is a task-dependent loss function.
The communication structure among clients is modeled as an undirected graph <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})</annotation></semantics></math>,
where each vertex <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to a client, and an edge <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math>. Clients are allowed to communicate only with their neighbors in <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(i):=\{\,j\in\mathcal{V}\mid(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}\,\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(i):=\{\,j\in\mathcal{V}\mid(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}\,\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Throughout this work, we assume a standard decentralized optimization setting in which the communication graph <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is connected and static, and communications are reliable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The most widely adopted framework for achieving decentralized training is based on <em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">gossip</em>.
In this paradigm, each client repeatedly alternates between optimizing its local model using local data and averaging the local model with neighboring clients to enforce consensus. For example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lian et al. (2017)</a></cite> propose DSGD, repeatedly performs local stochastic gradient updates followed by weighted averaging of neighboring models.</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\theta_{i}^{t+1}\leftarrow\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}w_{ij}\big(\theta_{j}^{t}-\eta\nabla f_{j}(\theta_{j}^{t})\big)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em" stretchy="false">←</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{i}^{t+1}\leftarrow\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}w_{ij}\big(\theta_{j}^{t}-\eta\nabla f_{j}(\theta_{j}^{t})\big),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the learning rate, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the gradient descent iteration index and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> are the mixing weights satisfying <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{ij}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{ij}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> if <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\in\mathcal{N}(i)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\in\mathcal{N}(i)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{ij}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{ij}=0</annotation></semantics></math> otherwise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">One of the central challenges in decentralized training is high communication cost.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koloskova et al. (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Islamov et al. (2025)</a></cite> reduce transmitted bytes via compression techniques such as sparsification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aji and Heafield, 2017</a>)</cite> or quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alistarh et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, but the overhead remains substantial for billion-scale models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Zeroth-Order Optimization</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Zeroth-order optimization provides a gradient-free alternative to backpropagation by estimating descent directions using only function evaluations.
Formally, given a loss function <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\theta;\mathcal{B})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\theta;\mathcal{B})</annotation></semantics></math> evaluated on a minibatch <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math> and parameters <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, zeroth-order methods approximate the gradient through randomized perturbations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following the <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al. (2023)</a></cite> formulation, the perturbation vector is drawn from a standard Gaussian distribution,</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Using the symmetric two-point estimator, the directional derivative along <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is computed from two loss evaluations at perturbed parameters:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\nabla}f(\theta^{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})=\frac{f(\theta^{t}+\epsilon z_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})-f(\theta^{t}-\epsilon z_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})}{2\epsilon}z_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mo>∇</mo><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\nabla}f(\theta^{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})=\frac{f(\theta^{t}+\epsilon z_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})-f(\theta^{t}-\epsilon z_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})}{2\epsilon}z_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> is perturbation scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Based on this gradient estimator, ZO-SGD iteratively performs the following descent step.</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{t+1}=\theta^{t}-\eta_{t}\,\widehat{\nabla}f(\theta^{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mo>∇</mo><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{t+1}=\theta^{t}-\eta_{t}\,\widehat{\nabla}f(\theta^{t};\mathcal{B}_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Zeroth-order methods can also be integrated into decentralized optimization, simply by replacing the local first-order update with a zeroth-order gradient estimate
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hajinezhad et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yi et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
As a result, most zeroth order decentralized algorithms share the limitation of gossip methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Shared Randomness as a Communication Primitive</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We assume that all clients have access to the same random number generator (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">RNG</span>), which enables any client to deterministically reconstruct the same perturbation vector from a given random seed.
Under this assumption, a zeroth-order update can be represented as a <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">seed–scalar pair</em> and deterministically reconstructed by any client.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, let the perturbation vector used by client <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> at iteration <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> be</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i,t}=\mathrm{RNG}(s_{i,t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>RNG</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i,t}=\mathrm{RNG}(s_{i,t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i,t}</annotation></semantics></math> is a random seed and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{RNG}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNG</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{RNG}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a synchronized random number generator shared across the network.
The corresponding scalar directional derivative is given by</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{i,t}=\frac{f(\theta_{t}+\varepsilon z_{i,t};\,B_{i,t})-f(\theta_{t}-\varepsilon z_{i,t};\,B_{i,t})}{2\varepsilon}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{i,t}=\frac{f(\theta_{t}+\varepsilon z_{i,t};\,B_{i,t})-f(\theta_{t}-\varepsilon z_{i,t};\,B_{i,t})}{2\varepsilon}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Thus, each zeroth-order update can be represented as a seed–scalar pair <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{i,t}=(s_{i,t},\alpha_{i,t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{i,t}=(s_{i,t},\alpha_{i,t})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Upon receiving <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{i,t}</annotation></semantics></math>, any client can reconstruct the perturbation vector and apply the corresponding update locally.
As a result, the size of each communicated update is independent of the model dimension <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>.
This representation fundamentally changes the communication model of decentralized training.
Once updates are seed-reconstructible, communication cost becomes negligible, and model dimensionality is no longer the primary scalability bottleneck.
Similar ideas have been explored in the context of centralized federated learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and fully connected distributed training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> for large language models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Nevertheless, most existing decentralized zeroth-order methods continue to rely on gossip-based averaging, implicitly assuming expensive communication.
In the next section, we show that this assumption becomes incompatible with seed-reconstructible updates and leads to prohibitive computational overhead.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18181v1/GossipvsFlooding4.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/268;" width="476" height="268"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Consensus dynamics of a single gradient under gossip-based model averaging (a) and flooding-based gradient dissemination (b). In gossip, time-varying gradient coefficients induce prohibitive aggregation cost. In contrast, flooding propagates each gradient with a fixed coefficient, without gradual diffusion, enabling uniform and fast application across
clients and leading to perfect consensus.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Limitations of Gossip</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given the communication efficiency enabled by shared randomness, a natural first attempt is to combine
seed-based communication with existing gossip-based decentralized training frameworks.
Instead of exchanging full model parameters, each client represents its local model as the accumulation
of all past updates <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, and communicates this history <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{i}^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{i}^{t}</annotation></semantics></math> in the form of a set of seeds and coefficients.
This representation can be written as</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{i}^{t}=\theta^{0}-\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{i}^{t}}c_{i,t}(m)\,\alpha(m)\,\mathrm{RNG}\!\bigl(s(m)\bigr)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mpadded style="width:2.296em;" width="2.296em"><mi>RNG</mi></mpadded><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{i}^{t}=\theta^{0}-\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{i}^{t}}c_{i,t}(m)\,\alpha(m)\,\mathrm{RNG}\!\bigl(s(m)\bigr),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where gossip-based averaging exchanges only the history set and performs model mixing by averaging the message coefficients,</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{i,t+1}(m)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}w_{ij}\,c_{j,t}(m),\qquad\forall m\in\bigcup_{j}\mathcal{M}_{j}^{t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">∈</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">⋃</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{i,t+1}(m)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}w_{ij}\,c_{j,t}(m),\qquad\forall m\in\bigcup_{j}\mathcal{M}_{j}^{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Representing a model update as a sum of gradient updates has also been adopted in prior centralized federated learning works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
At iteration <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, this approach requires communicating all updates generated by all clients up to that point.
Since each update is a constant size seed–scalar pair, the total communication cost scales as <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(tn)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(tn)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of clients, which is significantly smaller than transmitting dense model parameters of dimension <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, gossip-based averaging repeatedly reweights past updates.
Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Shared Randomness as a Communication Primitive ‣ 3 Method ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (a) illustrates this behavior. A single update generated by client <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is repeatedly reweighted and reapplied as it diffuses through the network. Under a seed-based representation, each change in coefficient requires reconstructing the corresponding perturbation from its seed and reapplying it to the model.
As the number of stored updates grows as <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(tn)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(tn)</annotation></semantics></math>, and applying each update costs <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(d)</annotation></semantics></math>,
the overall computation scales as <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(tnd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(tnd)</annotation></semantics></math>, which is prohibitively expensive.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As a result, combining seed-based communication with gossip shifts the scalability bottleneck
from communication to computation.
Once updates are seed-reconstructible, <em id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">gossip is no longer a suitable consensus primitive</em>:
When the communication object shifts from models to individual gradient updates, maintaining gradual diffusion via model gossip primarily increases the computational cost of applying updates.
In this setting, it is natural to consider an alternative in which each update is applied exactly once with a fixed coefficient across clients.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Flooding as a Consensus Primitive</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the structural mismatch of gossip under seed-reconstructible updates, we replace gossip-based averaging with flooding-based dissemination <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kshemkalyani and Singhal, 2011</a>)</cite>.
In flooding, each update is forwarded to all neighbors upon first reception and propagated across the network without further modification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We propose <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood, a decentralized training framework that disseminates zeroth-order updates using flooding.
Each time a client computes a zeroth-order update from its local data, the update is packaged as a seed–scalar pair and injected into the network.
Upon receiving a previously unseen message, a client forwards it to its neighbors, ensuring that the update propagates to all reachable nodes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A key property of flooding is that each update is reconstructed and applied exactly once per client.
Unlike gossip, flooding does not modify update coefficients across rounds, thereby eliminating repeated reconstruction overhead.
Moreover, the cost of flooding depends only on the number of newly generated messages, and is independent of the number of flooding step. By repeating flooding for a number of steps equal to the network diameter, all clients receive all updates generated in the same iteration.
Functionally, this realizes an all-gather–like dissemination of gradients per iteration, without transmitting high-dimensional tensors.
As a result, consensus error does not increase with network distance, and global synchronization is achieved even under sparse and irregular topologies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">At this stage, <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood resolves both major scalability barriers of decentralized training—communication cost becomes independent of model size, and consensus no longer degrades with network diameter.
However, seed-reconstructible communication introduces a new challenge: as the number of clients grows, each client must apply an increasing number of zeroth-order updates per iteration, which can incur substantial computation overhead.
In the next section, we address this bottleneck by introducing a computation-efficient zeroth-order gradient aggregation mechanism.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Computation-Efficient Gradient Aggregation</h3>

<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">

<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

<p id="alg1.13" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="alg1.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">for<span id="alg1.13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <em id="alg1.13.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="alg1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0\dots T-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0\dots T-1</annotation></semantics></math> in parallel <math id="alg1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall i\in[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall i\in[n]</annotation></semantics></math></em> </span>do</span></p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div>
<div id="alg1.14" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="alg1.14.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.14.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">  </span><span id="alg1.14.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">/* </span><span id="alg1.14.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">(A) Subspace setup for SubCGE<span id="alg1.14.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">  */</span><span id="alg1.14.4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">if</span></span><span id="alg1.14.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><em id="alg1.14.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;"><math id="alg1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\bmod\tau=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>mod</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\bmod\tau=0</annotation></semantics></math></em><span id="alg1.14.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="alg1.14.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">then</span>
</div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_many">
<div id="alg1.15" class="ltx_listingline ltx_figure_panel"><span id="alg1.15.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.15.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">   </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.15.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">  Initialize RNG with seed (</span><math id="alg1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\text{glob}}+t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mtext mathsize="0.900em">glob</mtext></msup><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\text{glob}}+t)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg1.15.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">

</span><math id="alg1.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}_{i}=\mathcal{R}_{i}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℛ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℛ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">∖</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒮</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}_{i}=\mathcal{R}_{i}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg1.19.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">

<div id="alg1.24" class="ltx_listingline ltx_figure_panel"><span id="alg1.24.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.24.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">   </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.24.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">   </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.24.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">  Sample </span><math id="alg1.m44" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i_{\ell},j_{\ell}\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{0,\dots,r-1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">∼</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">Unif</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">r</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i_{\ell},j_{\ell}\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{0,\dots,r-1\}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg1.24.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">

</span>
</div></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_many">
<div id="alg1.25" class="ltx_listingline ltx_figure_panel"><span id="alg1.25.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.25.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">   </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.25.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">  </span><span id="alg1.25.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">else</span>
</div></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_many">
<div id="alg1.26" class="ltx_listingline ltx_figure_panel"><span id="alg1.26.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.26.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">   </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.26.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">   </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.26.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">  Sample </span><math id="alg1.m46" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{\ell}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)^{\mathrm{shape}(\theta_{\ell})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">z</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒩</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">shape</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">θ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{\ell}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)^{\mathrm{shape}(\theta_{\ell})}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg1.26.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
