<div id="alg1.27" class="ltx_listingline ltx_figure_panel"><span id="alg1.27.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span><span id="alg1.27.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">  </span><span id="alg1.27.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">return</span><span id="alg1.27.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><em id="alg1.27.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;"><math id="alg1.m47" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z=[z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{L}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z=[z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{L}]</annotation></semantics></math></em><span id="alg1.27.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> ;  </span><span id="alg1.27.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">// </span><span id="alg1.27.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">RNG for SubCGE</span>
</div></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_many">
<div id="alg1.28" class="ltx_listingline ltx_figure_panel">
</div></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With global dissemination of seed-reconstructible updates, each client receives updates from all other clients.
Even under flooding-based dissemination, this requires applying <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n)</annotation></semantics></math> updates per iteration.
The cost of applying all these updates—which include regenerating the random perturbation vector and performing a descent step on the model—-grows quickly as the number of message increases.
This overhead can critically limit the scalability of <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this, we propose <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ubspace <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C</span>anonical-basis <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">G</span>radient <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">E</span>stimation (<span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span>), an aggregation-efficient representation of perturbation vector.
The key role of <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> is to reduce the cost of processing a large number of zeroth-order update messages under flooding, making the aggregation cost independent of the number of clients.
<span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> defines a low-rank subspace that is shared across all clients and restricts perturbation vectors to the canonical basis directions of the shared subspace.
Within this shared subspace, each perturbation and gradient corresponds to exactly one canonical coordinate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt a layer-wise subspace construction.
For each 2D layer <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times m_{\ell}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we maintain globally shared matrices
<math id="S3.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times r}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times r}</annotation></semantics></math>,
with entries sampled from <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> and specified via shared random seeds.
Perturbations are sampled from the canonical basis of this subspace.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Concretely, a perturbation takes the form</p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{\ell}^{(i,j)}=U_{\ell}e_{i}e_{j}^{\top}V_{\ell}^{\top}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{\ell}^{(i,j)}=U_{\ell}e_{i}e_{j}^{\top}V_{\ell}^{\top},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(i,j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(i,j)</annotation></semantics></math> is sampled uniformly from <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[r]\times[r]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>r</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[r]\times[r]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As a result, given <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> zeroth-order updates with coefficients
<math id="S3.SS4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k=1}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k=1}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, the aggregated update for layer <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> can be written as</p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\theta_{\ell}=U_{\ell}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}E_{i_{k}j_{k}}\right)V_{\ell}^{\top}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\theta_{\ell}=U_{\ell}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}E_{i_{k}j_{k}}\right)V_{\ell}^{\top},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p5.2" class="ltx_p">which can be applied with cost <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n+rd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n+rd)</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(nd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(nd)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">From an optimization perspective, <span id="S3.SS4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S3.SS4.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> is equivalent to rank-1 LOZO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> with a restricted perturbation pool.
In standard rank-1 LOZO, perturbations take the form</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\theta_{\ell}=uv^{\top}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>v</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\theta_{\ell}=uv^{\top},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p6.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> are typically sampled from normal distributions.
In contrast, <span id="S3.SS4.p6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S3.SS4.p6.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> restricts <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> to be selected from the column vectors of predefined random matrices <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> whose entries are drawn from a normal distribution. 
In practice, the speedup mainly comes from replacing numerous memory-bound axpy operations with batched matrix multiplications, which are far more efficient on GPUs.
Please refer Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Implementation Details and Runtime analysis of SubCGE ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> for implementation details.
As a result, <span id="S3.SS4.p6.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S3.SS4.p6.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> decouples the number of received updates from the cost of applying them,
making large-scale decentralized zeroth-order training computationally feasible.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, <span id="S3.SS4.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S3.SS4.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> is orthogonal to the choice of communication primitive.
While it is introduced in the context of <span id="S3.SS4.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.SS4.p7.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood, the aggregation bottleneck it addresses arises in any zeroth-order method that relies on a large number of seed-reconstructible updates. <span id="S3.SS4.p7.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S3.SS4.p7.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> can be readily combined with centralized or federated learning frameworks that employ shared randomness, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2024)</a></cite></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span><span id="S3.SS5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.SS5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood: Algorithm Overview</h3>

<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.14" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.15" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Comparison of communication overhead and consensus properties
in decentralized training.
<math id="S3.T1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>: number of clients, <math id="S3.T1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>: model parameter dimension, <math id="S3.T1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>: number of iterations,
<math id="S3.T1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>: subspace rank, with <math id="S3.T1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\gg t&gt;n\geq r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≫</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\gg t&gt;n\geq r</annotation></semantics></math>.
<math id="S3.T1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math> <em id="S3.T1.15.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Shared Randomness</em> indicates that updates are communicated as seed–scalar pairs.
<math id="S3.T1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ddagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>‡</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ddagger</annotation></semantics></math> Costs marked as prohibitive become infeasible at large model or network scales.</span></figcaption>

<td id="S3.T1.16.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-top:-0.45pt;padding-bottom:-0.45pt;"><span id="S3.T1.16.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Gossip with SR</span><sup id="S3.T1.16.1.3.1.2" class="ltx_sup"><math id="S3.T1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.800em">†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math></sup></td>
<td id="S3.T1.16.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:-0.45pt;padding-bottom:-0.45pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(tn)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">n</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(tn)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S3.T1.16.1.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:-0.45pt;padding-bottom:-0.45pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(tnd)^{\ddagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">d</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.800em">‡</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(tnd)^{\ddagger}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S3.T1.16.1.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:-0.45pt;padding-bottom:-0.45pt;"><span id="S3.T1.16.1.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">–</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.16.1.4" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;">
<td id="S3.T1.16.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:-0.45pt;padding-bottom:-0.45pt;"><span id="S3.T1.16.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;">S<span id="S3.T1.16.1.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">eed</span>F<span id="S3.T1.16.1.4.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">lood (ours)</span></span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.16.1.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:-0.45pt;padding-bottom:-0.45pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m20" class="ltx_Math" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" alttext="\mathcal{O}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" mathsize="0.800em">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" mathsize="0.800em">n</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(n)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S3.T1.16.1.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:-0.45pt;padding-bottom:-0.45pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m21" class="ltx_Math" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" alttext="\mathcal{O}(n+rd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" mathsize="0.800em">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" mathsize="0.800em">n</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" mathsize="0.800em">+</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" mathsize="0.800em">r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" mathsize="0.800em">d</mi></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(n+rd)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S3.T1.16.1.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:-0.45pt;padding-bottom:-0.45pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m22" class="ltx_Math" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" alttext="\checkmark" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFEBEB;" mathbackground="#FFEBEB" mathsize="0.800em">✓</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\checkmark</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18181v1/overall_12panels_ring_meshgrid.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/142;" width="476" height="142"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Task performance vs. Communication cost plots on diverse tasks in the SuperGLUE benchmark.
<span id="S3.F3.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.F3.10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood consumes near-zero communication cost (Kilobytes), and is spotted in the left of all panels.
<span id="S3.F3.10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.F3.10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood also records reasonably high task performances;
it outperforms existing communication-efficient rival baselines such as ChocoSGD or LoRA variants, while stays competitive to first-order methods such as DSGD.
While the absolute performance levels seem to vary slightly between different tasks, <span id="S3.F3.10.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.F3.10.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood consistently remains as a strong alternative in this trade-off.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.4 Computation-Efficient Gradient Aggregation ‣ 3 Method ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes <span id="S3.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S3.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood.
At each iteration, each client proceeds as follows.
(A) Subspace setup: every <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> iterations, the shared low-rank matrices <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> are re-initialized using a global random seed, resulting in identical subspaces across clients.
(B) Local gradient estimation:
each client independently samples a minibatch and a local random seed, generates a seed-reconstructible perturbation from the canonical basis via <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{RNG}_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNG</mtext><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{RNG}_{S}</annotation></semantics></math>, and computes a zeroth-order update represented as a seed–scalar pair.
(C) Flooding and aggregation: the update is flooded across the network, where each client filters previously seen messages, logs new ones, and applies the newly received updates in an SGD-style step.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.5 SeedFlood: Algorithm Overview ‣ 3 Method ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the communication and computation costs of decentralized training.
Traditional gossip incurs prohibitive communication cost, while gossip with shared randomness shifts the bottleneck to update application.
In contrast, our method achieves perfect consensus with <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(n)</annotation></semantics></math> communication and <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(n+rd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(n+rd)</annotation></semantics></math> update cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section provides a systematic evaluation showing that <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood can be a strong alternative to existing methods for large-scale decentralized training, with extremely small communication cost and near-zero overhead consensus.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Datasets and Models</span> Following the previous work on zeroth-order methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> we evaluate <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood on a subset of the SuperGLUE benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarlin et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and the SST-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Socher et al., 2013</a>)</cite>.
A total of 1,024 training samples are uniformly partitioned across all clients, while a shared validation set of 500 examples and a test set of 1,000 examples are used for evaluation.
We use models from the OPT family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> as the running language model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Procedure</span>  We evaluate decentralized training under ring and mesh-grid network topologies
to expose topology-dependent behavior.
For the total number of local optimization steps, we run 5,000 local iterations for zeroth-order methods and 500 iterations for first-order methods.
Using a larger number of iterations for ZO optimization is standard practice due to the higher variance of ZO gradient estimators compared to FO gradients <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
While many decentralized methods adopt a 1:1 ratio between local updates and communication rounds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lian et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koloskova et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, we instead perform 1 communication round every 5 local update steps, which is the highest frequency feasible with large language models and our compute constraints.
Since <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood incurs negligible overhead with respect to the number of flooding steps, we perform flooding for the number of steps equal to the network diameter at every iteration.
For ChocoSGD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koloskova et al., 2019</a>)</cite> with communication compression, we adopt 99% Top-<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> sparsification, representing the highest compression ratio considered in prior studies.
All other hyperparameters and training details are configured the same as those of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al. (2023)</a></cite> as reported in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Experiment setup ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation Metrics</span>  We report the Global Model Performance (GMP) scores, obtained by evaluating the average of all client models at the end of training, which is a standard metric in decentralized optimization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Communication Cost</span>  To account for the different iteration budgets used by first-order and zeroth-order methods, we compare all methods using the total communication cost transmitted over each network edge during the entire training process.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate decentralized training with network of 16 OPT-1.3B models.
We include DSGD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lian et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, the most basic decentralized learning method, and its zeroth-order counterpart, DZSGD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, as baseline methods.
In addition, we compare against ChocoSGD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koloskova et al., 2019</a>)</cite> with communication compression and LoRA variants of all methods, where only LoRA parameters are trained and communicated, as communication-efficient decentralized training approaches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.5 SeedFlood: Algorithm Overview ‣ 3 Method ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the task-wise performance of each baseline and <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood, along with the communication cost on a logarithmic scale.
<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood is extremely communication-efficient, requiring only 400 KB over the entire training process.
While ChocoSGD with 99% sparsification and LoRA-based variants reduce communication by approximately 50<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> and 1000<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> compared to full-parameter baselines, their communication cost still scales linearly with the model size, and remains more than three orders of magnitude larger than <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood.
In contrast, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood achieves model-size–independent communication by transmitting only random seeds.
As a result, even as model size increases and the communication cost of other methods grows accordingly, the communication cost of SeedFlood remains constant.
This property makes <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood scalable regardlessly of model size.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In terms of performance, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood outperforms the zeroth-order baselines DZSGD and DZSGD-LoRA on nearly all tasks with an exception of WiC.

This improvement is particularly pronounced under sparse network topologies, where efficient global information propagation becomes critical.
While baseline methods exhibit noticeable performance degradation when transitioning from mesh-grid to ring topologies, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood shows little sensitivity to network topology; as a result, it achieves relatively higher performance under sparse topologies due to its topology-invariant perfect consensus.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to DSGD, which incurs substantially higher communication cost (526 GB), <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood shows only a moderate performance gap of 4–6%.

This gap reflects the known sample inefficiency of zeroth-order optimization due to noisy gradient estimates, a behavior that has been consistently reported in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.


Notably, <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood also outperforms Choco-LoRA, the most communication-efficient first-order baseline (18 MB), by approximately 4%, indicating that communication-efficient gossip alone is insufficient to ensure strong consensus under limited bandwidth.
The detailed results for each experiment are reported in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Supplementary Task-Level Results for Large Networks ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood trades additional computation and a moderate accuracy gap for dramatically reduced communication, making it a competitive alternative in communication-constrained decentralized training settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Scaling for Larger Networks</h3>

<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18181v1/delta_bar_ring_mesh.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/248;" width="476" height="248"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Relative GMP differences (percentage points) from the 16-client baseline as the network size increases, comparing ring (left) and meshgrid (right) topologies.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T2.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.T2.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">
Relevant performance (%) on OPT-125m across different network sizes.
All values are normalized by DSGD with 16 clients. Bold indicates the best performance for each number of clients.
As the network size grows, the performance of other methods deteriorates, whereas <span id="S4.T2.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.T2.10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood remains robust and even outperforms first-order methods at 128 clients.
</span></figcaption>
<div id="S4.T2.11" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:168.5pt;vertical-align:-82.2pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(22.6pt,-11.0pt) scale(1.15091355168088,1.15091355168088) ;">

<tr id="S4.T2.11.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.11.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:-0.4pt;padding-bottom:-0.4pt;">
<table id="S4.T2.11.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T2.11.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.11.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:-0.4pt;padding-bottom:-0.4pt;"><span id="S4.T2.11.1.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">#Clients</span></td></tr>
</table></td>
<td id="S4.T2.11.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:-0.4pt;padding-bottom:-0.4pt;">
<table id="S4.T2.11.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T2.11.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.11.1.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:-0.4pt;padding-bottom:-0.4pt;"><span id="S4.T2.11.1.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">DSGD</span></td></tr>
</table></td>
<td id="S4.T2.11.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:-0.4pt;padding-bottom:-0.4pt;">

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next study the scalability of <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood under large and highly distributed networks.
By achieving perfect consensus with negligible communication overhead, <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood remains insensitive to network size, making it well suited for large-scale decentralized training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate scalability, we conduct experiments with OPT-125M over <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{16,32,64,128\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{16,32,64,128\}</annotation></semantics></math> clients.
The training data are evenly partitioned such that each client holds <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{64,32,16,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{64,32,16,8\}</annotation></semantics></math> samples, respectively.
All other settings follow the decentralized training protocol described in previous sections.
Due to computational constraints, experiments are performed on three tasks: SST-2, RTE, and BoolQ.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The relevant performance which is normalized by the 16-client DSGD is summarized in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Scaling for Larger Networks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
The complete results are reported in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Supplementary Task-Level Results for Large Networks ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.
Notably, in large-scale scenarios with up to 128 clients, <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood achieves performance comparable to,
and in some cases exceeding, first-order decentralized methods.
Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Scaling for Larger Networks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows the performance trends as the network size increases.
While all first order based gossip baselines exhibit performance degradation with more clients,
<span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood maintains stable performance and, in some cases, even shows slight improvements.
We attribute this behavior to reduced variance in zeroth-order estimation as more perturbations are aggregated across clients.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18181v1/runtime_vs_msgs.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/302;" width="405" height="302"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Runtime measurements for applying multiple zeroth-order gradient messages on OPT-2.7B using a single A100 GPU.
<span id="S4.F5.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S4.F5.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> is several orders of magnitude faster than MeZO.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18181v1/subcge_ablation_sst2_rte.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/169;" width="476" height="169" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F6.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F6.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Sensitivity of <span id="S4.F6.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S4.F6.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> to the subspace rank and refresh period on SST-2 (left) and RTE (right). Restricting the search space to an overly small subspace throughout training degrades performance, as shown in the upper-left region of the figure.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Effectiveness of <span id="S4.SS4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S4.SS4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A naive flooding can overflow the amount of information to aggregate and process in <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Scaling for Larger Networks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we find that the naive reconstruction of gradients based on MeZO can be overwhelmed by a growing cost of aggregating gradients, quickly dominating the overall runtime.
In contrast, <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> maintains low and scalable aggregation overhead, remaining orders of magnitude faster than MeZO even with thousands of gradient updates.
These results highlight <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> as a key enabler of practical decentralized training under flooding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For a sanity check, we finetune OPT-2.7B in a single-client setting and directly compare the results against MeZO.
Here, the subspace update interval is set to 500 iterations, and the subspace size is fixed to be 32.
As seen in <a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.3 Scaling for Larger Networks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span> shows no meaningful performance degradation compared to MeZO, and in some cases performs slightly better.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We further show that a sufficiently wide subspace is required for stable training, as small ranks and short refresh periods are associated with noticeable performance degradation (see <a href="#S4.F6" title="In 4.3 Scaling for Larger Networks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).
Moreover, overly frequent subspace refreshes can also harm performance; for example, we observe suboptimal results on RTE under short refresh periods.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Delayed Flooding</h3>

<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18181v1/partialflood.svg" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/248;" width="476" height="248"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S4.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Task performances on SST2 and RTE under partial flooding with varying number of flooding steps.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood assumes that messages are flooded across the entire network with diameter <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> at every local iteration.
In practice, the network diameter may be unknown, and full flooding can be infeasible under asynchronous execution and network delays.
To relax this assumption, we introduce delayed flooding, where the number of flooding steps <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is treated as a hyperparameter.
At each local iteration, messages are propagated up to <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> hops, while newly received messages continue to be forwarded in subsequent iterations.
Functionally, this corresponds to applying other clients’ updates with a bounded delay of at most <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lceil D/k\rceil" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌉</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lceil D/k\rceil</annotation></semantics></math> iterations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate delayed flooding by training OPT-125M on a ring topology with 32 clients, using <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
As shown in <a href="#S4.F7" title="In 4.5 Delayed Flooding ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood exhibits no observable performance degradation for moderate values of <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\geq 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\geq 4</annotation></semantics></math>), maintaining performance comparable to full flooding and consistently outperforming DZSGD.
This indicates that the benefit of flooding-based global aggregation does not rely on strictly enforcing perfect consensus at every iteration,
but rather on sufficiently fast global propagation of update information.
When <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is reduced to extreme values (<math id="S4.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=1</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>), performance degrades and falls below DZSGD, which we attribute to excessive staleness.
Overall, <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood remains effective as long as global updates propagate within a bounded delay, even without full flooding.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We address a fundamental scalability barrier in decentralized training: achieving reliable global consensus under severe communication constraints when model sizes are large.
<span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood makes a new attempt to address this challenge by enabling global dissemination of seed-reconstructible zeroth-order updates, making consensus independent of both model dimension and network topology.
By exploiting shared randomness, communication cost becomes negligible, and flooding realizes all-gather–equivalent synchronization at each communication round.
To make this regime computationally feasible, we introduce <span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>ub<span id="S5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CGE</span>, which removes the aggregation bottleneck induced by large numbers of zeroth-order updates.
Our extensive experiments demonstrate that <span id="S5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="S5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood enables robust training at scale, particularly under large networks and extreme data fragmentation, unlocking a new promising avenue for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. Specifically, our proposed method significantly reduces the communication overhead required for decentralized training. This improvement has the potential to lower the barrier to entry for training large-scale models and improve the energy efficiency of distributed learning systems. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, and yet, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.</p>
</div>
</section>

<span class="ltx_bibblock ltx_bib_cited">Cited by: <a href="#S4.SS1.p1.1" title="4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">§4.1</span></a>.
</span></li>
<li id="bib.bib31" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_article"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_author-year ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">Zhao <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">et al.</span> (2022)</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_author">H. Zhao, B. Li, Z. Li, P. Richtárik, and Y. Chi</span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_title">BEER: fast <math id="bib.bib31.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1/T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1/T)</annotation></semantics></math> rate for decentralized nonconvex optimization with communication compression</span>.
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_journal">Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_volume">35</span>, <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_pages">pp. 31653–31667</span>.
</span>

<a href="#S4.SS1.p2.1" title="4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">§4.1</span></a>.
</span></li>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Implementation Details and Runtime analysis of SubCGE</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide implementation details of SubCGE and a detailed breakdown of its runtime components.
In our implementation, each two-dimensional weight matrix maintains an additional buffer of the form <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{\ell}A_{\ell}V_{\ell}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{\ell}A_{\ell}V_{\ell}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.
During training, all coordinate-wise updates are accumulated into <math id="A1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the full update <math id="A1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{\ell}A_{\ell}V_{\ell}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{\ell}A_{\ell}V_{\ell}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> is applied to the base weight on-the-fly during the forward pass.
This design reduces the cost of applying received messages to <math id="A1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n)</annotation></semantics></math> and shifts the <math id="A1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(rd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(rd)</annotation></semantics></math> matrix multiplication cost to the forward pass.
Moreover, operations required for generating and updating perturbation vectors—which account for approximately 25% of the gradient estimation cost in MeZO—are replaced with lightweight coordinate updates under SubCGE.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details and Runtime analysis of SubCGE ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents a detailed runtime comparison between SubCGE and MeZO.
For each zeroth-order method, the total runtime is decomposed into gradient estimation and message application phases.
The cost of applying multiple messages further consists of random number generation and arithmetic operations for parameter updates.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">SubCGE follows MeZO’s procedure only for a small number of one-dimensional tensors, while for two-dimensional tensors it performs coordinate updates on the buffer <math id="A1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>.
In the gradient estimation phase, the additional <math id="A1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(rd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(rd)</annotation></semantics></math> matrix multiplication required to inject buffer values into the model slightly increases the forward-pass time; however, this overhead is offset by the substantially reduced perturbation cost.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, although SubCGE has a theoretical computation complexity of <math id="A1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n+rd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n+rd)</annotation></semantics></math>, our implementation effectively eliminates the computation overhead of message application in practice, with the additional <math id="A1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(rd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(rd)</annotation></semantics></math> computation largely hidden by the efficiency gains in perturbation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A1.T4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="A1.T4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Detailed wall clock time per iteration of the <span id="A1.T4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span>eed<span id="A1.T4.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">F</span>lood framework under
MeZO and SubCGE. Results are averaged over 5 steps on OPT-2.7B with
batch size 16 and 16 clients (i.e., 16 ZO-gradient messages generated
per iteration). “GE” denotes the gradient estimation phase, and “MA”
denotes the message-applying phase.</span></figcaption>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Experiment setup</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>dataset</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to computational constraints, we evaluate our method on a subset of SuperGLUE tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarlin et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
For experiments with OPT-1.3B using 16 clients, we consider BoolQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, MultiRC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khashabi et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, ReCoRD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, RTE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dagan et al., 2005</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bentivogli et al., 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Giampiccolo et al., 2007</a>)</cite>, and WiC<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pilehvar and Camacho-Collados, 2019</a>)</cite>, and additionally include SST-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Socher et al., 2013</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For experiments with OPT-125M and larger client counts {16, 32, 64, 128 }, we restrict evaluation to SST-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Socher et al., 2013</a>)</cite>, BoolQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, and RTE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dagan et al., 2005</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bentivogli et al., 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Giampiccolo et al., 2007</a>)</cite> to ensure feasibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For each task, we randomly sample 1,024 training examples and distribute them uniformly across clients. We use a fixed global validation set of 500 examples and a test set of 1,000 examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We use the same prompts as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al. (2023)</a></cite> for all tasks, and apply them consistently across both zeroth-order and first-order methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Hyperparameters</h3>

<figure id="A2.T5" class="ltx_table">

Validation loss is evaluated every one-tenth of the total training iterations, and the model achieving the best validation loss is selected for evaluation on a held-out test set.
</span></figcaption>

</figure>
<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the hyperparameter settings used in Sections 4.2 and 4.3. Following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we do not apply momentum and weight decay to local SGD updates. To ensure feasibility under limited computational resources, all baseline methods are configured to exchange communication every five local iterations. While increasing the number of local iterations can reduce communication overhead, overly large local steps are known to degrade performance; therefore, we adopt the smallest local iteration count permitted by our computational budget. All experiments use a constant learning rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For full-parameter tuning of ChocoSGD, we initialize surrogate model parameters with pretrained weights, which yields substantial performance improvement.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For SeedFlood, we fix the subspace rank and refresh period without additional search. Specifically, experiments in Section 4.2 use a rank of 32 with a refresh period of 1000, while those in Section 4.3 use a rank of 64 and a refresh period of 5000. Since the total number of training iterations is 5000, this effectively corresponds to using a fixed subspace throughout training. For zeroth-order methods, the perturbation scale is set following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al. (2023)</a></cite>. All other training-related settings not explicitly mentioned follow the configuration of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malladi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>LoRA configuration</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For all LoRA-based experiments, we adopt a fixed LoRA configuration. Specifically, we set the LoRA rank to 8 and the scaling factor
<math id="A2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> to 16. LoRA adapters are applied to the query and value projection layers (<span id="A2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">q_proj</span> and <span id="A2.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">v_proj</span>) of the transformer. We use a LoRA dropout rate of 0.05 across all experiments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Ablation Setup</h3>

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the SubCGE ablation study, we conduct 20K training iterations on a single OPT-2.7B client.
In the overall performance experiments, the subspace rank and update interval are fixed to 32 and 500, respectively, without additional search.
For the hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, we evaluate subspace ranks in
8,16,32,64 and update intervals in 50,500,1000,2000,20000, where an interval of 20000 corresponds to no subspace update during training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All other settings, including prompts, hyperparameters, and learning rate search procedures, follow the same experimental setup.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Supplementary Task-Level Results for Large Networks</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Task-Level Results for Large Networks ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Task-Level Results for Large Networks ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix C Supplementary Task-Level Results for Large Networks ‣ SeedFlood: A Step Toward Scalable Decentralized Training of LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> provide task-level results for the experiments that are not included in the main text. SeedFlood-8step denotes a variant of SeedFlood that executes only eight flooding steps. Overall, SeedFlood demonstrates competitive performance and, in large-scale settings with 128 clients, often outperforms first-order methods.</p>
</div>

    target="_blank" rel="nofollow">view the build logs</a>
    for errors. Generated by
    <a href="https://math.nist.gov/~BMiller/LaTeXML/" target="_blank" class="ltx_ref ltx_LaTeXML_logo">
      <span style="letter-spacing: -0.2em; margin-right: 0.1em;">
        L
        <span style="font-size: 70%; position: relative; bottom: 2.2pt;">A</span>
        T
        <span style="position: relative; bottom: -0.4ex;">E</span>
      </span>
      <span class="ltx_font_smallcaps">xml</span>
      <img alt="[LOGO]"
        src="data:image/png;base64,">
    </a>.
  </div>
  <div class="keyboard-glossary">
    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
